Hydrogen and its blend in Reheat Combustion

Detailed-chemistry DNS of hydrogen/methane flames at reheat gas-turbine conditions, and a high-order dimensionality-reduction method.

Sequential, or “reheat”, gas turbines burn fuel in two stages. In the second stage, fuel is injected into hot vitiated gas from the first and burns largely by spontaneous ignition. These combustors are a promising route to burning hydrogen for carbon-free power. In practice two modes coexist: spontaneous ignition in the hot bulk flow, and flame propagation in the cooler layers near the walls, which is also what controls flashback. How the balance between them shifts with operating pressure and fuel blend had not been quantified, even though burners are often developed with atmospheric-pressure tests.

For my M.Tech (Research) at IISc Bangalore, with Prof. Konduri Aditya, I studied this with detailed-chemistry DNS. The work was a collaboration with SINTEF Energy Research, ZHAW and Sandia’s Combustion Research Facility.

Temperature in the simplified reheat combustor from a 2-D DNS of a hydrogen flame at 5 bar.

Simulations

  • Solver: the massively parallel S3D code, a fully compressible solver with 8th-order central differences and 4th-order Runge–Kutta time stepping. It uses mixture-averaged transport through CHEMKIN and TRANSPORT.
  • Chemistry: a 9-species, 21-reaction mechanism for hydrogen and a 21-species, 42-reaction reduced San Diego mechanism for hydrogen/methane blends.
  • Configuration: a simplified reheat combustor with a mixing duct opening into a combustion chamber, isothermal 750 K walls and turbulent inflow from a channel-flow DNS. The flame is resolved by at least 35 grid points, with 5–22 μm grid spacing.
  • Parametric study: nine cases covering 1, 5 and 10 bar and hydrogen fractions of 100%, 70% and 50%. Inlet temperatures were adjusted to keep the ignition delay, and hence the flame position, fixed.
  • Analysis: chemical explosive mode analysis (CEMA) classifies each point as auto-ignition, assisted ignition (flame propagation) or extinction, so the fuel consumed by each mode can be measured directly.
  • Systems: SahasraT (IISc), Fram (Sigma2, Norway), Summit (OLCF) and Cori (NERSC).
Left: the simplified reheat combustor and its multi-block layout. Right: instantaneous temperature (K) from an earlier 3-D DNS of this configuration (top, Aditya et al. 2019) and from the 2-D DNS in this study (bottom).

Key findings

2-D DNS are a cheap, reliable guide to trends. Compared with full 3-D DNS, the 2-D simulations produce a W-shaped flame instead of a V-shaped one, because of a thinner thermal boundary layer. The bias in the fraction of fuel burned by spontaneous ignition, however, is only about 10%. That bias can be accounted for, so affordable 2-D DNS can screen many burner variants and operating points early in design.

Higher pressure shifts combustion toward flame propagation. At 1 bar, about 90% of the hydrogen is consumed by spontaneous ignition. At 10 bar the two modes consume comparable shares, with assisted ignition, or propagation, slightly ahead.

Combustion modes from CEMA (green: auto-ignition; red: assisted ignition; blue: extinction) and the fraction of fuel consumed in each. Left: 1, 5 and 10 bar. Right: hydrogen/methane blends, labelled (pressure in bar, H₂ fraction).

More hydrogen does the same. As the hydrogen fraction rises, the share of fuel burned by spontaneous ignition falls and propagation grows, more strongly at 5 bar than at 1 bar. This is counter-intuitive, since hydrogen is far more reactive than methane. It happens because methane-rich blends need hotter reactants to hold the flame in the same place. Since near-wall flame propagation controls flashback, atmospheric-pressure tests can understate how a hydrogen burner behaves at full load. That matters for designing hydrogen-ready reheat combustors.

Co-kurtosis PCA for reduced-order chemistry

Detailed chemistry makes these simulations expensive, and standard principal component analysis (PCA), the usual way to compress the thermochemical state, can miss rare but critical events such as ignition kernels. I co-authored co-kurtosis PCA (CoK-PCA), which takes its principal directions from the fourth-order joint moment (the co-kurtosis tensor) instead of the covariance, so it picks up these extreme-valued, stiff dynamics. On ethylene–air auto-ignition and ethanol HCCI-engine datasets, it reconstructs species production and heat-release rates more accurately than PCA where the chemistry is active.

A synthetic dataset with a small cluster of extreme-valued samples. Principal vectors from PCA (red) follow the bulk variance; those from CoK-PCA (blue) point toward the anomalous event.
